<header class="mast">
<div class="eyebrow"><span>Datum Line &#183; White paper</span><span class="acc">AI &#215; Bio &#183; September 2026</span></div>
<h1><span class="acc">Control</span> is an illusion.</h1>
<p class="sub"><span class="grn">Confidence</span> without control: scientific background and industry position.</p>
<div class="byline"><a class="back" href="./">&#8592; all documents</a> &#183; Kat Titterton &#183; San Francisco &#183; 25 September 2026</div>
</header>

<section class="abstract"><h2 class="lab">Abstract</h2>
<p>Every result in cell biology is a difference from a control, and nothing checks the control against anyone else&#8217;s. On the public JUMP Cell Painting dataset, a classifier names the institution from untreated wells alone <b class="acc">96.2%</b> of the time against 14.3% chance, so &#8220;normal&#8221; is a lab-specific coordinate, not a shared one. The standard batch corrections that make cross-lab discovery possible erase that coordinate (per-batch whitening drops lab identity to 12%, below chance): right for discovery, wrong for quality control. Datum Line keeps the coordinate and uses it. A lab&#8217;s control-well images are placed against the published field and every lab running the same line, and the lab gets back a certificate, a distance, and the direction of any shift. The bet still to be proven is that label-free brightfield carries the same signal as five-stain fluorescence; the test is specified and pending.</p></section>

<h2><span class="num">1</span>The control problem</h2>
<p>A control removes what a plate shares, including the plate&#8217;s own state, so a sick plate hides behind its own controls. Write a measured well as a shared mean, a plate state, and a treatment effect that may depend on that state:</p>
<div class="eq"><span class="m">x<sub>test</sub> = &#956; + s + &#964;(s)</span><span class="gap"></span><span class="m">x<sub>ctrl</sub> = &#956; + s</span><span class="gap"></span><span class="m">&#916; = x<sub>test</sub> &#8722; x<sub>ctrl</sub> = &#964;(s)</span><span class="eqn">(1)</span></div>
<p>The state <span class="m">s</span> cancels from the number but not from the cells. If <span class="m">s</span> is off, <span class="m">&#916;</span> is still computed, still looks clean, and is measured on cells that are not the ones the field has in mind.</p>
<p>The same logic nests upward: well inside plate, plate inside batch, batch inside site, site inside the field. Each control sees only inside its own box. A whole plate off is visible to the batch; a whole site off is visible to nobody in the building. Only a reference outside every box, the field, can see where a lab sits.</p>
<p>This is not an exotic failure. Irreproducible preclinical research costs about $28B a year in the US alone, and the largest single contributor, about 36%, is biological reagents and reference materials <a class="ref" href="#r1">[1]</a>. Cells are the input nobody certifies against anyone else&#8217;s.</p>

<h2><span class="num">2</span>Morphological profiling as a sensor</h2>
<p>An image of a cell is an unbiased, many-dimensional sensor: it answers &#8220;is anything about this run off?&#8221; rather than one hand-picked question. Cell Painting multiplexes six fluorescent dyes in five channels to mark eight cellular components, and automated analysis measures about 1,500 features per cell: size, shape, texture, intensity <a class="ref" href="#r2">[2]</a>.</p>
<p>At scale, the reference already exists. The JUMP Cell Painting Consortium (ten pharmaceutical companies, six technology partners, two non-profits) profiled over 116,750 compounds plus gene knockouts and overexpressions, all in U2OS cells <a class="ref" href="#r3">[3]</a>. Its main compound set, cpg0016, was produced across 11 sites, which is exactly the variation a cross-lab reference needs, and it is public under CC0 <a class="ref" href="#r3">[3]</a>.</p>
<p>The sensor is not the bottleneck. Many widely used bioactivity benchmarks are predicted well by simply counting cells, because their assays track cell health <a class="ref" href="#r5">[5]</a>. When a naive baseline matches a model, the comparison is the problem, not the model. In the author&#8217;s hepatocyte work, three feature extractors (CellProfiler, a CNN, a ViT) performed similarly <a class="ref" href="#r6">[6]</a>. The asset is the reference, not the extractor.</p>

<h2><span class="num">3</span>Evidence on public data</h2>
<p class="lead">Untreated wells carry their lab&#8217;s fingerprint, and the normalizations built for discovery erase it.</p>
<figure><div class="fighead"><span class="fn">Fig. 1</span> Lab identity from untreated wells, before and after correction</div><svg viewBox="0 0 680 204" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Lab identity accuracy under four conditions" style="display:block;max-width:680px"><text x="208" y="32" text-anchor="end" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="13" fill="#14171a">Raw features, held out by plate</text><rect x="220" y="18" width="384.8" height="20" rx="3" fill="#be1e74"/><text x="612.8" y="33" font-family="Archivo, sans-serif" font-weight="600" font-size="15" fill="#be1e74">96.2%</text><text x="208" y="72" text-anchor="end" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="13" fill="#14171a">Permuted labels</text><rect x="220" y="58" width="60.8" height="20" rx="3" fill="#b7bec1"/><text x="288.8" y="73" font-family="Archivo, sans-serif" font-weight="600" font-size="15" fill="#666e72">15.2%</text><text x="208" y="112" text-anchor="end" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="13" fill="#14171a">Per-plate standardised</text><rect x="220" y="98" width="56.0" height="20" rx="3" fill="#b7bec1"/><text x="284.0" y="113" font-family="Archivo, sans-serif" font-weight="600" font-size="15" fill="#666e72">14%</text><text x="208" y="152" text-anchor="end" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="13" fill="#14171a">Per-batch whitening (TVN)</text><rect x="220" y="138" width="48.0" height="20" rx="3" fill="#b7bec1"/><text x="276.0" y="153" font-family="Archivo, sans-serif" font-weight="600" font-size="15" fill="#666e72">12%</text><line x1="277.2" y1="10" x2="277.2" y2="174" stroke="#0f8f6c" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="277.2" y="192" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="13" fill="#0f8f6c">chance 14.3%</text></svg><figcaption>Balanced accuracy naming one of 7 institutions from vehicle-only JUMP wells; 12,046 wells, 3,781 features, folds held out by plate. results/e1.</figcaption></figure>
<div class="tw"><table><thead><tr><th>Plate 1053600681</th><th>Result</th><th>File</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Within-plate DMSO dispersion</td><td>79th percentile of 28; no local QC rule fires</td><td>results/e1</td></tr><tr><td>Wells named as their labelled lab (lab 2)</td><td><b class="acc">0 of 384</b></td><td>results/e1</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p><b>Space.</b> The plate above passes every check its own lab can run, yet every one of its 384 vehicle wells sits in another institution&#8217;s territory. Local QC cannot see this by construction (section 1).</p>
<figure><div class="fighead"><span class="fn">Fig. 2</span> Even one lab drifts</div><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Distance between two runs of the same cells against the gap between runs: rises from 0.74 same-day to about 2.3 at 6 to 13 weeks, then plateaus."><figcaption>Distance between plate centroids of the same cells, in units of within-plate spread; one institution, 31 plates, 8 runs, June to October; same-day reference 0.74 (n = 27). results/e1b.</figcaption></figure>
<p><b>Time.</b> Within one institution, the distance between two runs of the same cells grows from 0.74 for same-day pairs to about 3.1&#215; that at 6 to 13 weeks, then stops: 2.30 then 2.12 in the last two bins. Drift is bounded, which is what makes a reference possible, and a lab&#8217;s own history stops being a valid comparison after about three months.</p>
<p><b>Why correction is not the answer.</b> Batch correction for image-based profiling has been benchmarked on JUMP across ten methods <a class="ref" href="#r4">[4]</a>; its purpose is to remove lab and batch differences so biology can be compared. That is right for discovery. For quality control it deletes the one coordinate that says where a lab sits.</p>

<h2><span class="num">4</span>Formalism</h2>
<p>Everything in section 3 is one of six operations on the same well vector, each a difference of means or a held-out classifier, so any lab can check it. Every well becomes an embedding, z-scored across the field:</p>
<div class="eq"><span class="m">e = &#966;(image) &#8712; &#8477;<sup>3781</sup></span><span class="gap"></span><span class="m">&#966; &#8712; {CellProfiler, CNN, ViT}</span><span class="eqn">(2)</span></div>
<div class="tw"><table><thead><tr><th>Operation</th><th>Definition</th><th>Role</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>1 &#183; Embedding</td><td><span class="m">e = &#966;(image)</span></td><td>the sensor; choice of <span class="m">&#966;</span> barely matters [6]</td></tr><tr><td>2 &#183; Lab classifier</td><td><span class="m">f : e &#8594; lab</span></td><td>does the lab leave a fingerprint (96.2%)</td></tr><tr><td>3 &#183; Certificate distance</td><td>eq. (3)</td><td>how far a plate sits from the field, and which way</td></tr><tr><td>4 &#183; Variance decomposition</td><td><span class="m">Var(e) = V<sub>model</sub> + V<sub>site</sub> + V<sub>batch</sub> + V<sub>plate</sub> + V<sub>well</sub></span></td><td>how much is instrument, site, batch</td></tr><tr><td>5 &#183; Residualize known variables</td><td><span class="m">e<sub>&#8869;</sub> = e &#8722; &#202;[e | c]</span></td><td>remove only what is known to be instrument</td></tr><tr><td>6 &#183; Morphology change</td><td><span class="m">&#948; = f(&#8214;e &#8722; E[e | vehicle]&#8214;)</span></td><td>size of a shift, for the known-answer test</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p>The certificate is a difference of two means in units of the field&#8217;s spread, conditioned on the recorded variables <span class="m">c</span> (cell line, plate type, microscope, and so on):</p>
<div class="eq"><span class="m">d = &#8214; E[e | plate] &#8722; E[e | field, c] &#8214;<sub>&#931;</sub></span><span class="eqn">(3)</span></div>
<p>Its direction names the features that moved; its negative points back toward the field. &#8220;Normal&#8221; is therefore a conditional expectation, <span class="m">E[x | every variable]</span>, and it is only as good as the variables recorded. JUMP records the instrument side (site, batch, plate type, microscope, objective, filter set, pixel size); it does not publicly record serum or media lot, passage, seeding density, dye lots or operator.</p>
<p><b>Discovery and QC want opposite things from the same vector.</b> Discovery wants invariance to the lab, so it aligns every plate to a reference before comparing. QC wants the lab coordinate, so it must never align it away.</p>

<h2><span class="num">5</span>Limits and open tests</h2>
<p class="lead">Four claims are not yet proven, and each has a named test that could fail.</p>
<div class="tw"><table><thead><tr><th>Open question</th><th>Test</th><th>What would falsify it</th><th>Status</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Does label-free brightfield carry the lab signal?</td><td>Re-run e1 on the brightfield planes of the same 12,046 wells</td><td>Brightfield near 14% chance: the certificate needs one stain</td><td><span class="pend">pending</span></td></tr><tr><td>Does a lab&#8217;s position change the answer for a fixed drug?</td><td>e8: 8 positive controls on 1,829 plates, 11 sources; effect vs the field&#8217;s, against control distance</td><td>Spearman near zero: cells differ but answers do not</td><td><span class="pend">pending</span></td></tr><tr><td>Is the fingerprint biology or instrument?</td><td>Variance decomposition, microscope model separated from site</td><td>Nearly all variance in <span class="m">V<sub>model</sub></span>: a calibration product</td><td><span class="pend">pending</span></td></tr><tr><td>Does drift generalize beyond one institution?</td><td>Repeat e1b at each partner site</td><td>Unbounded drift elsewhere: no stable reference</td><td>one site</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p>Already controlled: vehicle-only wells (no compounds, so no treatment signal to leak), folds held out by plate, a permuted-label baseline at chance (15.2%), and the result surviving removal of the 1536-well source.</p>

<h2><span class="num">6</span>Industry position</h2>
<p class="lead">The market checks cell identity and ignores cell behaviour. Datum Line is the behaviour half, held by nobody who sells cells, media or instruments.</p>
<div class="tw"><table><thead><tr><th>Offering today</th><th>What it proves</th><th>What it cannot see</th><th>Relation</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>STR authentication</td><td>which line it is</td><td>same fingerprint, different behaviour</td><td>complement: identity, then behaviour</td></tr><tr><td>Vendor certificate of analysis</td><td>the lot shipped to spec</td><td>your incubator, after passage</td><td>complement</td></tr><tr><td>Instrument software, plate controls</td><td>the plate against itself</td><td>a whole plate, batch or site off</td><td>reads the same images</td></tr><tr><td>Phenomics platforms, batch correction</td><td>biology, lab removed on purpose</td><td>the lab coordinate, by design</td><td>collaborator: discovery upstream</td></tr><tr><td>Eyeballing and cell counts</td><td>gross death or overgrowth</td><td>texture and shape at equal counts</td><td>what labs do now</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p><b>Who pays.</b> Academic labs and cores, on every new line (at stake: the paper). Pharma and CRO screening groups, on every transfer (at stake: the screen; one line checked late cost about $2.6M in the author&#8217;s experience: 3 runs a week for 17 weeks at about $50k a run). Cell banks and vendors, on every lot (at stake: the lot and every lab that bought it).</p>
<p><b>Why it compounds.</b> Day one needs no network: the public JUMP reference already holds seven institutions&#8217; U2OS controls, so the first customer is compared with the field, not with an empty database. Every upload widens the reference, and bad-lot detection needs many labs on the same lot, so the later products exist only once the network does.</p>
<p><b>Price.</b> Per line, per quarter, set by the drift plateau: one reading covers its whole useful life. The figure is not yet set. <b>What leaves the building:</b> untreated control-well images only; no compounds, targets or results.</p>

<h2><span class="num">7</span>Roadmap</h2>
<figure><div class="fighead"><span class="fn">Fig. 3</span> Each phase opens only when the test before it passes</div><div class="road"><div class="stage" style="border-color:#be1e74"><b style="color:#be1e74">Certificate</b><span>U2OS vs JUMP</span></div><div class="gate"><span>gate</span>brightfield e1 above chance<i>&#8594;</i></div><div class="stage" style="border-color:#14171a"><b style="color:#14171a">3-site proof</b><span>protocol advice</span></div><div class="gate"><span>gate</span>3 labs uploading one line<i>&#8594;</i></div><div class="stage" style="border-color:#14171a"><b style="color:#14171a">Bad-lot flags</b><span>across labs</span></div></div><div class="side"><div class="stage" style="border-color:#0f8f6c"><b style="color:#0f8f6c">Reference built to break</b><span>planted failures; feeds the benchmark that grades bad-lot detection</span></div></div><figcaption>Gates are falsifiable tests from section 5; size and budget of the reference set are not yet set.</figcaption></figure>
